title: The mole and Avogadro's number

draft.title: The mole and Avogadro's number
card: Atoms and molecules are far too small to count one by one. Chemists use a counting unit called the mole (symbol mol).
One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles. This number is called Avogadro's number. The particles can be atoms, molecules or ions.
The number of particles = moles × 6.022 × 10²³. So 2 mol of any substance holds twice as many particles as 1 mol.
A mole is a fixed number of particles, not a fixed mass. Because a mole of a substance has a mass that can be measured, chemists can count particles by weighing.
draft.remember: One mole is always 6.022 × 10²³ particles, whatever the particles are.

a.q: Which statement about 1 mol of oxygen molecules and 1 mol of carbon atoms is correct?
opts: They contain the same number of particles
a.why: One mole of any particles is 6.022 × 10²³ of them, so both amounts contain the same number of particles. Mass is not what a mole fixes, so the same mass is a tempting but wrong choice.
a.clue: A mole is a number of particles, not a mass.

b.q: A sample of copper contains 3.0 mol of copper atoms. Which expression gives the number of atoms in the sample?
b.why: Number of particles = moles × 6.022 × 10²³, so the answer is 3.0 × 6.022 × 10²³, about 1.8 × 10²⁴ atoms. Dividing would give fewer than one mole's worth of particles, but 3.0 mol must hold more than 1 mol.
b.clue: More moles means more particles, so multiply.

a.best: They contain the same number of particles
